newsitem.title: IRELAND: EU ministers set to slam U.S. trade laws.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers set to slam U.S. trade laws.

text.p: EU foreign ministers, witholding support for President Bill Clinton's bombing of Iraq, were set on Sunday to deliver Washington a second snub with a sharp criticism of U.S. trade laws against Cuba, Iran and Libya.

The ministers began a second day of informal talks under Ireland's European Union presidency with the focus on how to retaliate against U.S. laws widely condemned for their potential to punish foreign companies that do certain kinds of business with the three states.
"We will be reviewing what retaliatory measures are open to us," Spanish Foreign Minister Abel Matutes told reporters.

European states are angry that their own companies risk becoming embroiled in U.S. attempts to punish Iran and Libya for its alleged support for terrorism and Cuba for its failure to democratise under Fidel Castro.
The sanctions are enshrined in two pieces of U.S. legislation -- the D'Amato act, which targets Iran and Libya, and the Helms-Burton laws, which are aimed at Cuba.

The EU has threatened to take the Cuba law to the World Trade Organisation. The European Commission has also drafted so-called blocking legislation to stop EU businesses complying with U.S. requirements.
Sunday's talks follow the failure of the ministers on their first day of discussions to give Washington backing for its attacks on Iraq to punish Saddam Hussein for an incursion into Kurdish areas.
EU ministers called on Iraq to withdraw from "safe havens" set up for Kurds after the 1991 Gulf War and said they backed the territorial integrity and sovereignty of all states in the region.
France had voiced reservations about Clinton's Iraqi raids, in stark contrast to the wholehearted support Washington received from Britain.
The EU said it wanted an oil-for-food deal with Iraq to go ahead as soon as United Nations Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali deemed that the situation on the ground merited it.
The deal would allow Iraq to sell a limited amount of oil, despite international trade sanctions, to buy badly needed food and medicine.

Following a briefing by international Bosnia mediator Carl Bildt, the EU ministers also agreed to a two-year peace transition period for Bosnia, a move diplomats said indicated the EU's intention to stay engaged in the region following September 14 elections.
Other items to be discussed on Sunday included the status of the bloc's treaty talks, the so-called inter-governmental conference (IGC)

Officials said the ministers would be given a report by the group negotiating the treaty. Ireland would also formally call a special EU summit for October 5 to discuss the IGC and other pending EU business.
IGC negotiators have been instructed to present a draft treaty to a second EU summit in Dublin in December.
